title: Life Sentences Tossed: Appeals Court Scraps Verdicts In Bizarre New Mexico Compound Exorcism Case
excerpt: A federal appeals court on Tuesday threw out all convictions tied to a remote northern New Mexico compound where a 3-year-old boy died in 2017 and adults
content:
A federal appeals court on Tuesday threw out all convictions tied to a remote northern New Mexico compound where a 3-year-old boy died in 2017 and adults engaged in tactical firearms training.

The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the kidnapping convictions against Hujrah Wahhaj, Subhanah Wahhaj, and Lucas Morton, barring prosecutors from retrying them on those charges. In the same ruling, the court vacated the terrorism-related convictions of Morton and Siraj Ibn Wahhaj, ordering a new trial on those counts due to a constitutional error during their proceedings.

All four defendants had previously been sentenced to life in prison following a joint federal trial in New Mexico.

The case originated in late 2017 when Siraj Ibn Wahhaj took his 3-year-old son, Abdul Ghani, from the boy’s mother, Hakima Ramzi, in Georgia. The child had severe medical needs, including cerebral palsy and frequent seizures. According to court records, the father and extended family members traveled from Georgia to Alabama and eventually established an off-grid desert compound near Amalia, New Mexico.

While there, adults in the group subjected the boy to daily rituals called ruqyah—described in trial records as “[a] Muslim version of an exorcism”—in an effort to rid him of evil spirits. During a final session in late December 2017, the child choked and stopped breathing. His remains were later discovered by law enforcement hidden inside an underground tunnel on the property.

In throwing out the kidnapping counts, the three-judge appellate panel ruled that prosecutors failed to prove the child was taken or held unlawfully under the federal kidnapping statute. Writing for the court, Circuit Judge Gregory Phillips noted that Siraj Ibn Wahhaj had lawful parental custody of his son when he took him from Georgia, and no existing custody order forbade the travel at that time.

The panel held that the trial judge misdirected the jury by instructing that the taking was unlawful merely if it occurred without the mother’s consent. Judge Phillips wrote that while the situation was an “unattractive [and] immoral situation” that ended in tragedy, federal law requires proof that a statute or court order was violated to constitute federal kidnapping. Because the government produced insufficient evidence on that legal element, double jeopardy protections prevent a retrial on the kidnapping and conspiracy to kidnap charges.

The appeals court also addressed the convictions against Siraj Ibn Wahhaj and Morton for conspiracy to kill federal officers and providing material support. Trial evidence showed the group believed the boy would be resurrected as Jesus Christ to lead an army against corrupt institutions, including the FBI and CIA, and had conducted weapons training to prepare.

While the panel found that prosecutors presented enough evidence to support the federal conspiracy claims regarding an attack on government institutions, it vacated the convictions because the trial court ‘breached the men’s Sixth Amendment rights.’

Both Siraj Ibn Wahhaj and Morton had chosen to represent themselves at trial. During deliberations, the jury sent out two substantive notes, including a question about whether proving an act in furtherance of a conspiracy required an automatic guilty verdict. The trial judge held a telephone conference with standby attorneys and decided to tell the jurors to simply reread their instructions, excluding the two self-represented defendants from the discussion entirely.

The appellate court deemed that exclusion a structural constitutional error, holding that it shut out the defendants during a critical moment of trial strategy.

The 10th Circuit remanded the terrorism and material-support counts against Siraj Ibn Wahhaj and Lucas Morton back to the U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico for retrial.
